notes.title: Update 0.4.4
notes.content: [p]With update [b]0.4.4[/b], we set ourselves a challenge: take your feedback, push further, and try something bold. This patch introduces some of the biggest shifts to Ashes of Morgravia so far - from deckbuilding to item progression - reshaping how every run feels.[/p][p][/p][h2]🃏 Deck Editor - Build Before You Begin[/h2][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45290708/b136af716e7a9ae4eed70f13062c9a785a015624.jpg"][/img][/p][p]We heard you out regarding your feedback. Now, you can edit your deck before each run. This is a major shift in how you approach the game: craft your deck to complement your gear and tailor strategies to your playstyle. Personally, it’s hard to imagine going back - it just feels right.[/p][p][/p][h2]📜 Unlockable Cards with Quests[/h2][p]A powerful deck should be earned. Cards in the editor now unlock through quests, giving you new goals to chase and ensuring your hands will be full for the foreseeable future.[/p][p][/p][h2]🌀 Ethereal Cards[/h2][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45290708/331d1e5d5b7b5369eed979c19ae2436f8d879324.jpg"][/img][/p][p]To complement the deck editor, all cards gained during the Desolation are now [b]Ethereal[/b] — they vanish when you return to the Sanctum. This keeps your edited deck meaningful while ensuring that each run feels fresh and self-contained.[/p][p][/p][h2]🎨 New Visuals[/h2][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45290708/21bd348f6742608744c709bc235a35a2da831ec2.png"][/img][/p][p]We rebuilt the [b]Sanctum[/b], item icons, and intro sequence from scratch. Everything now feels more cohesive and aligned with the atmosphere of Morgravia’s dark world.[/p][p][/p][h2]🛡️ Run Penalties Rework[/h2][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45290708/ab1a21ce5b4b2a5013d8c51cef7ef1b3ea1c7a88.jpg"][/img][/p][list][*][p][b]No more downgrades on death.[/b] Dying should sting, but not spiral you into a punishment loop. This change makes runs fairer without removing tension.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Healing in the Sanctum.[/b] Returning restores you to full health.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Torment & heal options removed.[/b] Since torment cards don’t carry over, there’s no need to burn them away anymore.[/p][/*][/list][p][/p][h2]⚖️ Balance & Progression[/h2][list][*][p][b]Cards and enemies rebalanced[/b] to better fit the new systems.[/p][/*][*][p][b]Upgrade costs increased.[/b] With no more downgrades, we’ve made upgrades pricier to preserve progression pacing.[/p][/*][/list][p][/p][h2]✨ Fresh Content[/h2][list][*][p][b]New items[/b] added - keep your eyes open.[/p][/*][*][p][b]New Sanctum music[/b] by the brilliant [b]Makai Symphony.[/b] The reworked visuals deserved a haunting new score, and this one gave us chills when speaking to the Harbinger.[/p][/*][/list][p][/p][h2]What’s Next[/h2][p]In the near future, we’ll be focusing on:[/p][list][*][p]Fixing known bugs.[/p][/*][*][p]Improving buff/debuff displays when enemies stand on adjacent vertical tiles (we already have a system planned).[/p][/*][*][p]Exploring a [b]set system for items[/b] - but we’ll keep the details close to the chest for now.[/p][/*][/list][p][/p][p]This update is another step toward making Ashes of Morgravia the deep, dark tactical journey we’ve envisioned - shaped by your feedback and our obsession with pushing it further.[/p][p][/p][p]Thank you for playing, thank you for sharing your thoughts, and as always:[/p][p]🕯️ Stay sharp, and never surrender to the Well.[/p][p]– The background blur. team[/p]

notes.title: Update 0.4.0
notes.content:
[p]We’re excited to share a major update to the [b]Ashes of Morgravia[/b] demo, and it’s a big one. [b]Your[/b] feedback has helped us shape this version into a more cohesive and satisfying experience. We look forward to hearing your thoughts.[/p][h3]Phase Fusion - One Flow, Two Decks[/h3][p]The most impactful change: we’ve [b]fused the Stride and Clash phases into one continuous flow[/b]. Don’t worry - the two-deck system remains. But now, you can [b]customize the ratio of Stride to Clash cards drawn each turn[/b], giving you more control while maintaining the tactical depth. This change massively improves pacing and onboarding without sacrificing strategy.[/p][h3]Real-Time Card Calculations[/h3][previewyoutube="5F4Z7XphtPc;full"][/previewyoutube][p]All cards now display their [b]real-time calculated values[/b] in your hand, factoring in all active buffs and debuffs. No more guesswork - you’ll know exactly how hard you’re hitting (or blocking) as you plan your next move. This improves the clarity and rhythm of each turn.[/p][h3]Card & Item Balance Pass[/h3][p]With the new system in place, we’ve rebalanced the majority of [b]cards and equipment[/b] to ensure a fair and enjoyable experience across builds. Expect tighter synergy, smoother scaling, and more viable paths through the Desolation.[/p][h3]✨ Quality of Life & Feedback[/h3][list][*][p][b]Save support[/b] added: your game now saves each time you [b]enter or exit the Sanctum[/b].[/p][/*][*][p]New [b]visual feedback[/b] for damage taken and healing received, making each moment on the battlefield more impactful.[/p][/*][*][p]You can now [b]sell your unused items[/b], making inventory management more meaningful and rewarding.[/p][/*][*][p]And, of course, [b]various bug fixes and improvements[/b] across the board.[/p][/*][/list][hr][/hr][p]This update is another step toward shaping [i]Ashes of Morgravia[/i] into the deep, dark tactical experience we envision - and we’re just getting started.[/p][p]Thank you for playing the demo. Your feedback is [u]everything[/u].[/p][p]
🕯️ Stay sharp, and never surrender to the Well.[/p][p]- The background blur. team[/p]

notes.title: Demo Quickfix #1
notes.content:
[h2]⚔️ Quickfix Update - Desolation Length Selection + More![/h2][p]We’re only a short while into the demo launch, but we already wanted to push an update that introduces a feature we’ve had in mind for a while - and we think it fits the game perfectly.[/p][hr][/hr][h3]🗺️ Choose Your Desolation Length[/h3][p]You can now [b]select the length[/b] of the Desolation before descending.[/p][p]Longer paths mean [b]greater danger[/b] - but also [b]greater rewards[/b].
This system is tied to progression:
You'll need to [b]complete earlier maps[/b] and [b]level up your Godwoken[/b] to unlock deeper, more punishing routes through the Desolation.[/p][p]We believe this shift strengthens the game’s core loop and gives more meaning to returning to the [b]Sanctum[/b] - upgrading your gear, preparing your deck, and making each descent count.[/p][hr][/hr][h3]🔊 Other Improvements[/h3][list][*][p]Adjusted and expanded [b]sound effects[/b] across the board[/p][/*][*][p]Minor tweaks and balancing updates[/p][/*][*][p]Stability improvements and polish[/p][/*][/list][hr][/hr][p]Thanks again for all the feedback, bug reports, and support.
Keep descending - and don’t forget to rest in your Sanctum when you can.
- The [i]Ashes of Morgravia[/i] Devs[/p]

tags.feature: You can now [b]select the length[/b] of the Desolation before descending.

notes.title: Dev Update #1
notes.content:
Greetings, wanderers of the dark! We’re back with an update on Ashes of Morgravia and its journey through development. Keep in mind that the numbers stated below are not final, and we are expecting them to multiply in the following months. 
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45290708/7ee3fa900f33f20fd75a2cf9fa673ecf2fd395f3.png[/img]
Here’s what we’ve been conjuring in the shadows:

🃏 Cards Galore:
 We now have 27 cards in total, with 17 more designed and awaiting implementation. Each card deepens the tactical choices and brings new flavor to every encounter.


✨ Boons Abound:
 There are 8 boons already in the game, with 11 more designed and ready to be added. These powerful blessings add layers of strategy and reward skilled play.


🦴 Horrors in the Night:
 We’ve created 7 enemy types so far, with many more monstrosities on the way. Expect each foe to challenge your wits and resourcefulness.


🗺️ A World to Explore:
 Our desolate landscapes include 3 maps with numerous variations, ensuring no two descents are ever the same.


🕯️ The Sanctum Awaits:
 At the heart of the game lies the Sanctum, a hub where players can upgrade gear, apply blessings, and prepare for the descent into the darkness. It's a place of uneasy refuge - and the only thing standing between you and the Well.


🛡️ Gear Up:
 There are already 25 unique items waiting to be discovered and equipped. These tools of survival will only continue to grow in variety and power.


We’re already deep into development, weaving together systems that will enhance the core gameplay loop and make every run feel rewarding and meaningful.
Playtesting is underway!
 If you’re interested in experiencing Ashes of Morgravia in its early stages, and helping us shape the game with your feedback - we’d love to hear from you!
The amount of content in the game will only continue to expand over the coming weeks, so stay tuned for more updates. The journey is just beginning.
The night is deep, and the way forward remains uncertain.

notes.title: From Tabletop to Digital
notes.content:
Game development is a constant process of [b]iteration, discovery, and compromise[/b]. What starts as one idea often morphs into something entirely different, shaped by testing, limitations, and instinct. [u]Ashes of Morgravia[/u] is no exception. In this devlog, we want to share the [b]key design decisions[/b] that shaped the game—from its earliest prototypes to the tactical dark fantasy deckbuilder it is today. [h2][b]The Sci-Fi That Never Was[/b][/h2] Believe it or not, [u]Ashes of Morgravia[/u] [b]was almost a sci-fi game[/b]. Initially, we envisioned a [b]futuristic setting[/b], where players would control a heavily armored mech, with its equipped modules influencing their deck. They would face off against relentless biomechanical monstrosities, a concept inspired by [u]Into the Breach[/u]. However, as we started testing the mechanics in a [b]tabletop format[/b], using [b]Skaven miniatures from Warhammer: The Old World[/b], we realized something wasn’t clicking. It wasn’t the mechanics—it was the [b]style and tone[/b]. Sci-fi felt too rigid, too defined by its world-building demands. We found ourselves naturally gravitating toward a [b]dark fantasy setting[/b], one that allowed for [b]instinctive, symbolic storytelling rather than technical explanations[/b]. The shift felt [b]right[/b]—and stylistically, it played to our strengths. Thus, [u]Ashes of Morgravia[/u] [b]embraced its gothic, Mörk Borg-inspired aesthetic[/b], a world where faith and corruption intertwine, where magic is both salvation and damnation. [h2][b]The Problem with Movement in Deckbuilders[/b][/h2] One of the biggest insights came from [b]playing other deckbuilders[/b]. We love the genre, but we noticed a recurring issue: [b]movement always felt slow and secondary[/b]. In most games, positioning wasn’t a true strategic factor—it was just [b]an action tax[/b]. This led us to a core design breakthrough: ✅ [b]What if movement was as important as combat?[/b]  ✅ [b]What if players had two decks instead of one?[/b] This was how the [b]Stride Deck and Clash Deck[/b] were born. Instead of treating movement as a minor mechanic, we gave it [b]its own deck[/b], forcing players to balance positioning [b]just as much as attacking[/b]. It was a natural evolution, reinforcing the [b]duality of the game’s themes[/b]—holy vs. profane, life vs. death, planning vs. reacting. [h2][b]The Challenge of Animated Cards[/b][/h2] The animated cards in [u]Ashes of Morgravia[/u] were, of course, inspired by [b]Gwent[/b]. They add [b]so much personality and atmosphere[/b]—but wow, did they slow down production. 😅 When we started, [b]we had zero experience with animations[/b], so it was a massive learning curve. [b]Would we do it again?[/b] Honestly… probably not. But now that they’re here, they [b]breathe life into the game[/b], making it visually distinct and far easier to market. So, even though they eat into our production time, they’re [b]a trade-off we’re ultimately happy with[/b]. [h2][b]The Influence of Bakhtin and Duality in Design[/b][/h2] On a more philosophical note, something that resonated deeply with the game’s design was [b]Mikhail Bakhtin’s concept of duality—particularly the idea of the carnival[/b]. The [b]constant cycle of chaos and order, reverence and mockery, destruction and renewal[/b]. This duality lined up perfectly with what we were building: 🔥 [b]Holy vs. Profane[/b] – Faith-based magic vs. corrupting power.  ⚔ [b]Life vs. Death[/b] – Healing miracles vs. sacrificial strength.  🃏 [b]Strategy vs. Instinct[/b] – Careful deck construction vs. adapting on the fly. None of this was [b]strictly intentional at first[/b]—but the more we refined the design, the more these [b]themes became instinctual[/b]. [h2][b]More Than Slay the Spire with Hexes[/b][/h2] Yes, [u]Ashes of Morgravia[/u] owes a lot to [u]Slay the Spire[/u], but we never wanted to just [b]copy the formula[/b]. We introduced [b]hex-based tactical combat[/b], where [b]positioning is just as important as cardplay[/b]. But beyond that, we also [b]rethought how power-ups work[/b].

[b]Boons: A Different Take on Power-Ups[/b]

Instead of relics, we have [b]Boons[/b], inspired by the progression mechanics of [u]Balatro[/u] and [u]Elden Ring[/u]. Boons are tied to [b]equipped items[/b] and redefine playstyles: [list][*]Some [b]passively enhance abilities[/b].[/*][*]Others [b]require Action Points to activate[/b], creating [b]risk-reward mechanics[/b].[/*][*]Each Boon fundamentally [b]shapes your build[/b], offering new synergies every run.[/*][/list] This small change added [b]another layer of depth[/b], making each playthrough feel [b]fresh and strategic[/b]. [h2][b]Cutting Scope: How Limitations Made the Game Better[/b][/h2] Like any indie team, we have [b]limited time and resources[/b] (we’re still juggling day jobs!). Originally, [u]Ashes of Morgravia[/u] had [b]a larger hub system, like Darkest Dungeon[/b], where players would manage a sanctuary between runs. But as development progressed, we realized: ⚠ [b]Too much downtime between battles made the game drag.[/b]  ⚠ [b]The hub system was fun, but it pulled focus away from the core experience.[/b] We pivoted to something [b]leaner and more dynamic[/b], focusing on [b]roguelike structure instead[/b]. And honestly? [b]The game is better for it.[/b] Sometimes, cutting features [b]doesn’t weaken a game—it strengthens its core.[/b] [h2][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/h2] [u]Ashes of Morgravia[/u] started as [b]a sci-fi tabletop prototype[/b] with [b]Skaven miniatures[/b]. It evolved into a [b]dark fantasy deckbuilder[/b] that tackles [b]duality, movement-driven strategy, and emergent storytelling[/b]. Along the way, we’ve had to make [b]compromises, unexpected discoveries, and design pivots[/b]—but that’s the beauty of game development. We’re excited for what’s next, and we’d love to hear your thoughts! What elements of the game excite you the most? Let us know in the comments! 👇
